title: How Bunk looked and ran the band
summary: Blumberg describes the band's look, Bunk's stare, stomping off tunes, replaying tunes for applause and pacing the evening.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I'd like to talk a little about Bunk. I mean, my impression of Bunk as he looked. I mean, I remember the band, of course, was all sitting down. The whole band had a marvelous look about it. Lawrence Marrero looked like a real rock of Gibraltar sitting there playing the banjo. I remember he looked like the steadiest beat in town, you know. Even if you didn't hear him, you knew that the guy had to have a steady beat because he absolutely had this immobile smile, a Buddha-like smile. And he was a great-looking fellow. And, of course, the horn players were sitting down in chairs behind their stands, and Bunk was wearing these high shoes. And he'd have his pants hiked up so you could see all these high shoes he wore and his long underwear. Yeah, long underwear in there. Always in the summer, I think, too. Yeah. I think so. And Bunk had a way of cocking his eyes over to one corner of the room when he'd play. He'd usually be looking up at a corner. Louis does very much the same thing. And it gave him a great look and went with the sound of the horn. But, I mean, a very striking stare. You'd really be seeing some eyeball there. Yeah. It would come along with the playing. And when he'd play a climbing phrase, an ascending phrase, his eyes would go up, you know, which would add to the effect of the whole thing. And he had a very interesting way. Well, he used to run the band very authoritatively. There was no doubt that he was running the band when you'd see him because he'd stomp his feet very loud, you know, to stomp off the tune, set the tempo.
Had you ever heard that anyplace else before?
No, I don't think I'd ever heard a scene that way of running a band with the pounding of the foot. And he would take the thing out with one pound of the foot.
We were talking the other night about you thought it's usually in the middle of the last chorus before the...
I think it depended on probably when he would decide to take the thing out. I think it would either be right before the last chorus.
That's what I thought usually. I would think that's the place they usually should give it and they're supposed to. But I think, too, sometimes they'd bunk and other people, too, in the middle of it.

There'd be a last-minute decision to take the thing out. And there'd be a pause between phrases and you'd hear this bang, you know. And bunk would kind of move his head when he'd stomp his foot, too. Kind of a twist, throw of the head like a, I don't know, I think of a thoroughbred horse gives a little throw of the head and a snort, you know. And bunk had a way of throwing his head just like that, you know. And he'd stomp his foot, he'd throw that one foot down and give his head that little throw, you know. And then play the thing out. And he had a wonderful way of running the band. When the crowd would be particularly pleased by a tune, if it was a fast tune, an exciting tune, he'd just stomp, as soon as the tune would be over and the people would start applauding, he'd stomp it off and start playing the same tune all over again. And I don't know if that's common practice down here.

Yeah, it always has been down here, I think. And still is, to some extent, if you've got a real New Orleans old-time group there, they'll have to play a tune twice again. Dances, maybe not so much at some of the nightclubs and sessions around.
Regular dance, they'll play them twice.
I remember that was a real surprise the first time.
They did that practically everything, because the crowd up there liked everything.
I think they'd applaud. Sometimes they'd go three, I've heard them three or four times on certain numbers.

Yeah, they'd go good on three or four times. They'd go right into what would correspond to maybe the third chorus from the last again, and then they'd take it two more out or something like that. And he would pace the band very well. He'd build up. He wouldn't let the band, I think, achieve too great an excitement early in the evening. He'd pace it. If the tunes were swinging along real well, but it was early in the evening, he'd kind of cut them short a little bit. So there'd be something left for later on. And I remember noticing that, how the thing seemed to build from the beginning of the evening right all the way through. It just kept getting more and more exciting each set. And you never got the feeling that the band was going downhill after a climax. It always seemed to be getting better. And that's when I realized that I had been listening to too many records and not enough in-person performances, because you can't get that concept of a band over the whole period of an evening from one tune on a record.
